tagline.text: A National Geological Monument cut between limestone peaks, with the historic Wawa Dam

location.label: Location
location.text: Wawa, Barangay San Rafael, Rodriguez (formerly Montalban), Rizal

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half a day to a full day

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,500 (including transport, entrance fee and guide, per person for a day trip)

children.text: Montalban Gorge is a limestone gorge in Rodriguez, Rizal, close to central Manila. Wawa Dam, which supplied Manila's drinking water starting in 1909, Mount Pamitinan, Mount Binacayan and historic caves sit together here, making it a great half-day nature outing.
Montalban Gorge is a water gap carved by the Marikina River at the western edge of the Sierra Madre, between Mount Pamitinan (about
) and Mount Binacayan (about

). The limestone mountains formed roughly 20 to 25 million years ago, and long erosion by water left a valley lined with white cliffs, marble boulders and huge blocks of stone. The gorge is reported to have been declared a National Geological Monument in 1983, and the whole area became the Pamitinan Protected Landscape (roughly 600 hectares) under Proclamation No. 901 in 1996.

Administratively the site belongs to Rodriguez, Rizal. Its former name was Montalban, so many people still say Montalban Gorge or Montalban Wawa Dam. Because there are two names, typing any of Wawa Dam, Montalban Gorge or Pamitinan into a map app brings up the same area. It is not far from the northeastern edge of Metro Manila, and it takes about
1–1.5 hours
from Quezon City by public transport.
The center of it all is Wawa Dam. The American colonial government began building it in 1904 and put it into service in 1909 as a water source for Manila. It is an arched gravity dam about

long. Angat Dam took over its role in the late 1960s and Wawa was retired in 1968. Today it is a recreation spot of calm reservoir, spillway wall and surrounding rocks. The main activities are bamboo raft rides on the reservoir above the dam, swimming among the rocks below it, climbing the two mountains and exploring caves.

The gorge has plenty of stories too. Legend says the giant Bernardo Carpio is wedged between the two mountains to keep them from crashing together, and Pamitinan Cave is said to be where the Katipunan gathered during the Philippine Revolution. Japanese and American forces also fought the Battle of Wawa Dam here from March to May 1945. Seeing nature and history together is what makes this gorge special. It has also appeared in films, and since July 2024 the Upper Wawa Dam project upstream has been underway, turning the area again into a setting for water supply and energy storage. That new facility is separate from the old Wawa Dam tourist site, so check which areas are open before you go.
This arched dam, completed in 1909, has water spilling over a wall roughly

high. The reservoir side is calm and good for photos, and in the rainy season the swollen water looks much more powerful. Walking along the dam and watching the morning light come in between the two mountains is the most popular scene.

On the reservoir you can take a bamboo raft or small boat run by local residents. It is the easiest way to see the cliffs on both sides up close. The price depends on the number of people and the route, so agree on it before you board.

Below the dam, the river runs past smooth marble boulders and shallow pools. However, the depth changes suddenly in places and the current is strong after rain, so only get in where locals are swimming. If you bring children, check locally whether life jackets can be rented.
This short but steep limestone mountain takes about
2 hours
to climb from Wawa village to the summit. Sharp rocks near the top call for gloves and shoes with good grip, and you must register and climb with a guide.
This National Geological Monument cave is reached by crossing a hanging bridge from the gorge. Its large chamber, the Bulwagan, lies about
inside the entrance by most accounts (guides vary), and the cave is said to have been a Katipunan meeting place. You need a flashlight and a guide.
Mount Binacayan faces Pamitinan and is about the same height. Rock climbers and boulderers visit as well, and hiking guides are available in the village.
Knowing the story of the giant holding up the two mountains makes the gorge more interesting. Locals also say earthquakes are the giant struggling.

blocks.title: Iron footbridge and boulder field below the dam

children.text: An old iron footbridge crosses the boulder field below the dam and makes a good photo spot with a view over the whole gorge. The rocks are smooth, so walk slowly, especially after rain.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: Wawa Dam and a stroll through the gorge

children.text: Take a jeepney or UV Express bound for Rodriguez from the Cubao area of Quezon City. Leave early to avoid the midday sun and the crowds.
Arrive at Wawa village, pay the entrance fee at the office and sign in. From the parking area to the dam it is a riverside path of about
10–20 minutes
on foot.
Admire the reservoir and the cliffs of the two mountains from above the dam and ride a bamboo raft.
Take photos on the rocks below the dam and only wade in safe, shallow spots.
Have lunch and rest at a restaurant or stall near the entrance.
Leave the village before the sun gets strong. Traffic back is heavy on weekend afternoons, so allow extra time.
This route centers on rafting and photos and is light on effort, so it also suits a family outing.
Leave at dawn, arrive at Wawa village, register at the office and barangay, then find a guide.
Start climbing Mount Pamitinan. The ascent takes about
2 hours
, and the rock near the summit is sharp.
Enjoy the summit view and come back down carefully the same way.
After lunch, go with your guide to Pamitinan Cave. Turn on your flashlight and head toward the Bulwagan.
Stop at Wawa Dam to rest by the water, then head down and go home before dark.
Parts of the cave may be off limits in the rainy season or when the water is high. Ask your guide about conditions that day first.
From Metro Manila, take a jeepney or UV Express bound for Rodriguez or Montalban from the Cubao area of Quezon City. A long-known alternative is to take a van from EDSA toward Eastwood and transfer.
From central Rodriguez to Wawa village, go by tricycle or jeepney. Often you ride only to the village entrance and then walk in to the dam.
It takes about
1–1.5 hours
from Quezon City and longer depending on traffic. Check current fares and routes locally.
If you arrive at Ninoy Aquino Airport, it is easiest to go to Quezon City first and transfer there.
From Marikina or the Batasan area, go through San Mateo into Rodriguez and follow the Wawa signs. Use the paid parking near the village entrance.
Taxis are rare. You can get there with a ride-hailing service such as Grab, but it may be hard to find a car for the return. Arranging a round-trip hire in advance is safer.
The November–May dry season is good for both hiking and swimming. In April and May, however, the heat is intense and the reservoir level drops, so the dam may look less impressive.
In the rainy season the swollen water is spectacular, but the current can suddenly speed up, so avoid swimming. Weekday mornings are the quietest, and weekends and holidays are crowded.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Best for trekking and raft rides
Move mostly in the early morning; water levels may be low
Swimming and climbing are riskier, so check conditions first

items.label: Entrance fee
items.note: Per person; no official fee schedule (2022 and 2025 visitor reports), confirm locally

items.label: Parking
items.note: Car about ₱30, motorcycle about ₱20 (2022 report); up to about ₱100 at some lots

items.label: Cottage (hut)
items.note: Space rental, peak season (2022 and 2025 reports); check the time and group size covered

items.label: Bamboo raft or boat
items.note: One boat, round trip of about 20 minutes (2022 report); varies by route and group size, agree before boarding

items.label: Mountain and cave guide
items.note: Hired after registering; confirm the price in advance

items.label: Public transport
items.note: Jeepney or UV between Cubao and Rodriguez; tricycle extra

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.

There are no large hotels near the dam, so most people visit as a day trip. If you need to stay, hotels in central Rodriguez or nearby Marikina and Antipolo are the realistic choice. The gorge area is poorly lit at night and the rocky paths are dangerous, so plan to leave before dark.
Stalls near the entrance sell fruit, Filipino snacks and samalamig (sweet cold drinks). Eat simply at a village restaurant, and look in central Rodriguez for more variety. Carry your trash out.

Even on a day trip, bring plenty of water and snacks. Shops at the village entrance sell bottled water and snacks, but prices can be slightly higher than in town. If you are climbing with a guide, you can save time by packing a lunch or by planning to eat at a village restaurant after you come down. Central Rodriguez has Filipino home-style restaurants, grilled chicken places and bakeries, which widens your choices. Long ago many visitors rented a hut at the Wawa Dam entrance and ate a packed lunch as a family, and you can still see the same scene on weekends.
Wear sneakers or sandals with a rough sole rather than slippers. Wet rock is extremely slippery.
Bring small bills in cash. Entrance, parking, rafts and lunch are mostly paid in cash.
Register at the office and go with a guide for the mountains and caves. Climbing alone is not recommended.
Bring a flashlight or headlamp for the cave. A phone light alone is not enough.
Swim only in the safe areas where locals swim, and not after rain.
Weekends are crowded, so a weekday early morning is better. If the weather has been bad, contact the Rodriguez tourism office before you leave.
Bring a waterproof phone pouch, spare clothes, a hat and 1–2 liters of water. There is not much shade.
Agree with your guide on the route, duration and cost before you start, and get a receipt or a note; this reduces disputes.
When taking photos, do not get too close to railings on the dam or the edges of rocks. Moss-covered rock easily makes shoes slip.
After rain, or when it rains upstream, the water in the gorge rises quickly. Stop swimming and climbing and check conditions.
Drownings are known to have occurred in this gorge. Be very careful when swimming.

In April 2023 the local government temporarily closed Wawa Dam to tourists after clashes between the military and armed rebels, and it has since reportedly reopened. Check the latest announcements about whether it is open and what the fees are before you visit.
The limestone near the summits of Pamitinan and Binacayan is sharp. Wear gloves and follow your guide.
It is dangerous at night because of poor lighting and many rocks. Come down before sunset.
The new Upper Wawa Dam construction zone nearby is different from the Wawa Dam tourist site. Follow the signs for the areas open to visitors.
Mobile signal may be weak in places, so agree on a meeting place and time with your group in advance.
This is a protected area in the same province of Rizal. It is known for reservation-only eco tours and is worth a separate day if your schedule allows.
This is Rizal's best-known city, with a pilgrimage church and restaurants with views. It is a candidate when you look for lodging and food near the gorge.
A town full of art studios and murals. It adds some urban atmosphere after a nature trip.
A swimming spot in the Tanay area of Rizal. You can add it when touring Rizal along with the gorge.
